Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Horizon Financial Group third quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review Horizon Financial Group's results for the third quarter of 2024. With me this morning are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Jennifer Lee, Chief Financial Officer; David Patel, Chief Risk Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Credit Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Horizon Financial Group delivered strong performance in the third quarter, driven by our commitment to customer service and operational excellence.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Growing our core businesses
2. Investing in technology and innovation
3. Managing risk effectively
4. Optimizing our capital allocation
5. Enhancing our employee engagement.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on our progress in key areas, including our deposit franchise dynamics, revenue diversification efforts, the assumptions behind our guidance, our capital strength, and risk-weighted assets optimization. These initiatives have positioned us well amid a challenging environment. Deposits grew solidly, reflecting relationship strength even as rates pressured costs. We've made significant strides in diversifying revenue toward higher-margin fees, our full-year guidance rests on a balanced macro view, capital ratios exceed requirements with room for returns, and disciplined RWA management supports efficiency. I'll now turn the call over to Jennifer Lee to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Jennifer Lee:
Thank you, Michael, and good morning. Horizon Financial Group reported net income of $1.2 billion for the third quarter, or $2.45 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 5% year-over-year due to loan growth and improved net interest margin. Non-interest income was up 15% year-over-year to $800 million. Key performance indicators include ROE of 12.5% and an efficiency ratio of 55%. We are confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me expand on some critical elements driving these outcomes, starting with our deposit franchise—specifically the dynamics around cost of deposits, average rates, and competitive pressures. Deposits remain the bedrock of our low-cost funding model here at Horizon Financial Group, with total deposits averaging $145.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4% quarter-over-quarter and 12% year-over-year, reflecting solid core relationship growth despite the elevated rate environment.

Our total cost of deposits rose to 2.85% in Q3, up 35 basis points sequentially from 2.50% in Q2 and 110 basis points year-over-year. This reflects the ongoing beta realization on our interest-bearing deposits, which came in at approximately 48% for the quarter—right in line with our guided range of 45-50% as the Fed funds rate holds steady around 5.33%. By beta cohort, our legacy deposits from pre-2022 are accruing at just 1.20%, while newer balances are pricing closer to 4.10%, highlighting the stickiness of our core franchise.

From a mix standpoint, non-interest-bearing demand deposit accounts—or DDAs—continue to anchor our low-cost profile, comprising 28% of the mix and accruing at a negligible 0.15%. Savings and money market accounts, at 52% of the mix, saw rates tick up to 2.95%, driven by competitive repricing on our flagship Horizon Rewards Money Market product. Time deposits, making up the remaining 20%, averaged 4.25%—up from 3.85% last quarter—as we rolled off $2.8 billion in brokered CDs maturing below 3.5% into higher-rate specials to maintain liquidity coverage ratio headroom above 130%.

The deposit market remains intensely contested, with national averages for 12-month CDs hovering at 4.75% per Bankrate data and high-yield savings accounts from fintech disruptors like Ally and SoFi advertising APYs north of 4.50%. Money market funds are yielding 5.20-5.40% on average, per iMoneyNet, pulling in roughly $200 billion in inflows year-to-date as investors chase yield amid sticky inflation. Among peers, we've seen JPMorgan Chase report deposit betas creeping toward 55% in their retail segments, while Wells Fargo noted elevated costs in their priority banking channels due to promotional brokered CDs. Regionally, pressure is most acute in our Northeast franchise—New York and Boston MSAs—where money-center competition from bulge brackets has pushed local CD rates 25-40 basis points above national averages, contributing to a 3.10% cost in that footprint versus 2.60% in our more stable Midwest markets like Ohio and Michigan. In the Southeast, where we're expanding via recent integrations, costs are moderating at 2.70% thanks to stronger relationship DDA retention from small business clients.

To counter these headwinds, we've implemented several targeted initiatives. Our dynamic pricing engine—powered by our partnership with Q2's deposit optimization platform—enabled real-time rate adjustments, capturing 15% more digital deposit inflows at targeted betas while avoiding overpayment on core balances. We launched a promotional 13-month CD ladder at 4.60% for balances over $250k, which gathered $1.2 billion in Q3 with an implied beta under 40%, and expanded tiered relationship pricing, offering up to 50 basis points premium yields for customers with combined balances exceeding $1 million. On the tech front, we've accelerated our mobile-first acquisition strategy, integrating Plaid APIs to streamline transfers from external high-yield accounts, driving a 22% increase in digital savings deposits. We're also actively managing our funding mix, reducing reliance on FHLB advances—which cost 5.40% this quarter—by 10% through targeted core deposit campaigns.

Strategically, our focus remains on mix shift and franchise value over short-term rate chasing. We've grown non-interest-bearing deposits by 7% quarter-over-quarter through enhanced cash management products like our Horizon Treasury Gateway, targeting C&I clients with sweep features linked to our commercial loan book. This has stabilized our loan-to-deposit ratio at 92%, providing ample capacity for sub-4% loan growth without liquidity strain. Looking forward, we expect Q4 deposit costs to rise another 20-25 basis points to around 3.05-3.10%, with betas moderating to 40-45% as repricing lapping slows. That said, NIM compression should peak this quarter at 3.25%, with expansion resuming in 2025H1 as asset yields reprice higher and deposit competition eases with potential Fed cuts.

Overall, our deposit beta trajectory and retention metrics—98.5% annualized core deposit beta stability—position us favorably versus peers, underscoring the durability of our $100+ billion core deposit base built over decades.

Shifting to revenue diversification initiatives and their impact, in an era of persistent net interest margin compression—now at 2.85% for Q3, down 15 basis points quarter-over-quarter amid inverted yield curves and deposit beta pressures—we've aggressively pivoted toward high-margin, recurring non-interest income streams. This isn't just about resilience; it's about sustainable growth in a Banking-as-a-Service world dominated by fintech disruptors like Stripe and Adyen, and peers like JPMorgan Chase scaling their asset management arms to over $3 trillion AUM.

Total revenue reached $14.2 billion, up 8% year-over-year, but the real story is in the mix: net interest income accounted for 58% of total revenue, down from 68% a year ago, while non-interest revenue surged to 42%, a record high and up 22% year-over-year. This shift delivered $2.1 billion in fee and trading income alone, representing a 250 basis point improvement in our non-interest revenue margin to 1.45%. Excluding one-offs like the $150 million gain from our Visa stake monetization, core non-interest growth was still 18%—outpacing NII by 3x and shielding EPS from the 5% NII headwind due to higher funding costs.

We've structured our diversification around four pillars: Wealth & Asset Management, Payments & Transaction Services, Corporate & Investment Banking fees, and Emerging Growth Verticals like ESG and digital assets.

In Wealth & Asset Management, rebranded as Horizon Wealth Solutions, client assets under management grew to $1.8 trillion, up 14% year-over-year, fueled by inflows of $120 billion—primarily from high-net-worth individuals and family offices shifting from passive index funds amid market volatility. We launched AI-driven personalization via our HorizonAdvisor Pro platform, leveraging machine learning models similar to BlackRock's Aladdin for dynamic portfolio rebalancing, boosting advisory fee revenue by 28% to $450 million. Cross-sell penetration into our 15 million retail deposit base hit 12%, driving $800 million in new recurring fees. Client retention improved to 96%, with margins expanding 50 basis points to 45 basis points on AUM.

Payments & Transaction Services revenue jumped 32% year-over-year to $1.2 billion, capturing share in the $2.5 trillion global real-time payments market. Our HorizonPay Global API ecosystem, PSD2-compliant in Europe and RTP-enabled in the US via The Clearing House partnership, processed 2.1 billion transactions quarterly, up 25%, with average fee per transaction rising 8% to $0.57 through premium treasury management tools like dynamic FX hedging—mirroring HSBC’s FXall platform. Embedded finance integrations with platforms like Shopify and Uber generated $300 million in new B2B revenue, diversifying beyond traditional card fees, now 40% of PTS versus 60% in 2022.

Corporate & Investment Banking fee momentum saw CIB fees rise 15% to $650 million, with investment banking fees up 20% on blockbuster deals like a $25 billion LBO advisory for a tech unicorn. We capitalized on syndicated lending trends, originating $180 billion in new facilities with 65% take-up in ESG-linked loans—yielding 120 basis points higher fees than vanilla structures. Trading revenues, bolstered by our rates and credit desks, added $400 million, flat year-over-year but with volatility-adjusted ROE at 25%.

In emerging verticals, we allocated $500 million from our capital plan to high-growth bets. Sustainable finance products, including green bonds and carbon credit trading, generated $250 million—up 50% year-over-year—positioned ahead of EU Taxonomy regs and Fed climate stress tests. In digital assets, our HorizonCrypto custody platform, regulated under NYDFS BitLicense, onboarded $15 billion in institutional crypto AUM, contributing $80 million in custody and staking fees, with partnerships accelerating adoption.

Geographically, North America, at 65% of non-interest revenue, saw stable 12% growth, driven by WAM and PTS amid Fed rate pauses, though deposit migration to money market funds pressured NII. EMEA, 20%, delivered 35% growth, leveraging open banking mandates, with PSD3 readiness via 500+ API partnerships adding €400 million in embedded finance fees. Asia-Pacific, 15%, showed 45% momentum, with $300 million from cross-border PTS in India and Southeast Asia via UPI interoperability and WeChat Pay integrations, originating 30% of APAC ESG loans.

Macro tailwinds include the digital payments TAM expanding at 15% CAGR through 2027, while NIM volatility pegged at 2.7-3.0% through 2024 necessitates 50%+ non-interest reliance. Diversification has de-risked our model: non-interest revenue volatility dropped 30% year-over-year, standard deviation now 8% versus 11%, and ROTCE held at 13.5% despite NII softness. Margins here are superior—60-70% versus 40% for NII—with lower capital intensity, freeing CET1 for buybacks.

Looking ahead, we target 45-50% non-interest mix by 2025, adding $3-4 billion annually through organic growth and tuck-in M&A. Risks include regulatory scrutiny on interchange fees and geopolitical FX swings, but our hedges cover 90% exposure. These initiatives position Horizon as a top-quartile performer versus peers averaging 35% non-interest reliance.

Before turning to other areas, let me outline the key assumptions underlying our full-year 2024 guidance, which we affirmed today: adjusted earnings per share of $8.75 to $9.25, representing 6-10% growth over FY2023; total revenue growth of 5-8%, driven by NII stabilization and non-interest expansion; and ROTCE of 12-13.5%. These targets assume no material M&A, no significant regulatory changes beyond anticipated, and execution on priorities.

Our guidance anchors in a soft landing for the U.S. economy, with real GDP growth of 2.0-2.5%—in line with New York Fed nowcasts—and core PCE inflation at 2.2-2.5% by year-end. We expect the Fed to deliver 75-100 basis points of cuts, fed funds at 4.25-4.75% by Q4 after the recent 50 bps cut. This supports NIM expansion of 5-10 bps in H2 as deposit beta normalizes to 35%—down from 45% in 2023—and loan repricing accelerates in commercial portfolios.

Globally, ECB rates ease to 2.75-3.25%, Eurozone GDP at 1.0-1.5%. Unemployment stays benign at 4.1-4.4% U.S. and 6.5% Europe, with net charge-offs up to 45-55 bps, concentrated in consumer credit cards and autos, where delinquencies hit 3.2% per FDIC.

On balance sheet, deposit growth of 3-5%, transaction accounts 4-6% via Plaid and Finastra integrations. Brokered CDs capped at 15%. Loans: C&I up 4-6% on middle-market capex; CRE flat to +2%, office under 5% stress-tested to 9% cap rates; consumer 2-3% at 6.5-7.0% mortgage rates. NII growth 4-7%, NIM to 3.40-3.55%. LCR above 130%, HQLA 115%.

Fee income targets 8-11% growth: WAM AUM up 7-9% to $450 billion on $20-25 billion inflows, equity returns 8-10%. Card fees 6-8% on 5% volumes. Capital markets +10-15% on $1.4-1.6 trillion issuance. Trading flat to +5% at VIX 18-22.

Expenses capped at 4-5% growth, positive jaw via $250 million gen-AI savings like Palantir AIP for fraud, AWS migration cutting mainframe 15%, tokenization pilots. Provisions 0.70-0.85%, CECL 1.20-1.25%. CET1 11.8-12.2% post-stress.

U.S. consumer resilience drives 60%, digital app users up 25% to 15 million. Europe 20%, PSD3 boosts embedded finance. Asia-Pacific 10%, 12-15% growth on UPI with PhonePe/GrabPay.

High-conviction: double private banking AUM to $100 billion; BaaS up 30% to fintechs like Chime/SoFi.

Risks: 50 bps deeper recession shaves 10-15% EPS; inflation delays compress NIM 10 bps; CRE distress buffered by 7.2% yields, 65% LTV. Geopolitics hits 5% flows. We'll update at Investor Day.

Turning to our capital position, our ratios remain a cornerstone of our fortress balance sheet. As of quarter-end, CET1 stands at 13.5% fully loaded Basel III, up 70 bps sequentially and 120 bps year-over-year, with a $52.4 billion base against $388 billion RWAs—a 2% reduction. Tier 1 is 15.8%, including $9.2 billion AT1 like high-trigger CoCos.

Regulatory minima: CET1 4.5% + 2.5% buffer = 7.0%, plus 1.5% G-SIB, 2.25% Pillar 2A from CCAR/DFAST (post-stress 10.8%), counterparty buffers total 11.75%—we're 180 bps above, targeting 200 bps management buffer. Tier 1 13.25%, 155 bps ahead.

U.S. (65% RWAs) at 14.2%, Europe (20%) 13.8% offset by hedging, Asia-Pacific (15%) 12.9% on CRE but defensive.

Trends: CET1 from 12.3% end-2022 via $6.8 billion organic from $18.2 billion NII up 22%, $4.5 billion buybacks reducing shares 3.2%, AOCI recovery. RWAs up 1% despite 8% loans via $12 billion auto ABS (40% relief), $3.2 billion energy offloads.

Basel III Endgame could add 10-15% RWAs; we model 70-90 bps CET1 hit to 12.6%, 110 bps above. IFRS 9 overlays, Stage 2 4.2%.

Capital fuels: 12% dividend hike to $1.28, 48% payout; $10 billion buyback, $3.5 billion left, $2-2.5 billion H1; $25 billion M&A capacity like recent $1.2 billion bolt-on. RWA optimization via AI IRB, AT1 refresh, low-RWA fees.

Fed cuts stabilize NIM at 3.45%, CRE buffers strong. Top-quartile resilience.

Finally, on risk-weighted assets management, total RWAs at $1.42 trillion, down 2.1% quarter-over-quarter and 0.8% year-over-year, driving CET1 to 12.8%, up 40 bps, above 11.5% target. Fully loaded 13.2% ex-Basel IV floors.

Credit RWAs (82%, $1.16 trillion) down 2.5% on $15 billion CRE derisking, office to 1.2% loans, PDs 2.1%. Market RWAs (10%, $142 billion) flat via SA-CCR, derivative compression $200 billion notional. Op RWAs up 1% to $122 billion contained by AMA.

Americas (45%) down 1.8% on $10 billion RMBS. EMEA (30%) down 3.2% on €8 billion syndications. Asia-Pacific up 1.5% mitigated by collateral.

IRB recalibrations 4% relief, $12 billion CLOs, CDS hedging 12% CVA cut, SEC-IRBA pilots. Basel IV adds $80 billion, stress-tested.

RWAs stabilize $1.40-1.43 trillion, unlocking $4 billion buybacks, 45 bps dividend hike, M&A, low-RWA fees up 15%.

This is our competitive moat.

Thank you. I will now turn it over to David for risk.

David Patel:
Thank you, Jennifer. As Chief Risk Officer, I would like to briefly discuss our risk management framework. We continue to prioritize proactive risk identification and mitigation. Our key focus areas include credit risk in commercial real estate, cybersecurity threats amid rising digital adoption, and climate-related exposures. We remain vigilant in monitoring emerging risks like geopolitical tensions and adapting our strategies accordingly, with enterprise-wide stress testing showing resilience across scenarios.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, as a reminder, that is [star one] to ask a question. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the outlook for deposit cost trends and betas into next year?

Michael Reynolds:
Good morning, John. Thanks for the question. As Jennifer detailed, we're seeing betas in line at 48% this quarter, with Q4 at 40-45% as repricing slows. Legacy stickiness at 1.20% and our pricing engine have helped, and with Fed cuts, we expect moderation, supporting NIM expansion in 2025H1. Our core base remains durable at 98.5% retention.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
What are your expectations for non-interest revenue growth and the non-interest mix heading into 2025?

Jennifer Lee:
Thanks, Emily. We're targeting 45-50% non-interest mix by 2025, with $3-4 billion added annually. Q3's 42% mix, up from 32%, came from WAM inflows, PTS transaction growth, CIB fees, and emerging like ESG/digital assets. Organic plus tuck-ins, with lower volatility, positions us strongly versus peers.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Robert Kim:
Can you comment on the credit quality of the commercial real estate portfolio, especially office?

Lisa Chen:
Good morning, Robert. Credit quality remains strong overall. CRE is tightly underwritten, office under 5% with 9% cap rate stress, LTVs at 65%, PDs low at 2.1% versus sector 3.5%. We've derisked via syndications and sales, with coverage 220%, no PDCCF needed. Delinquencies stable, reserves adequate at CECL 1.20-1.25%.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to Michael Reynolds for any closing remarks.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for your interest in Horizon Financial Group. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
